steps.title: The warehouse and its fleet
steps.say: An invented fulfilment centre, 160 by 59 metres: 123 single-width aisles holding 1,476 pick faces in three storage blocks, two-cell travel highways between groups of aisles, 20 pack stations along the bottom, and 250 robots from three invented vendors parked at the top beside 24 chargers. Each robot's battery comes with its charge-cycle history; a fade model fitted on it is scored on the last 120 days it did not see, against each pack's own trend, and names the packs that will reach 80% within six months.

steps.title: A peak order wave
steps.say: The generator is told the evening peak has begun: 9,000 orders an hour, more than the fleet can finish. Each order arrives as a pick face with a 10-minute SLA. Every three seconds the dispatcher (CP-SAT over free robots, open orders and pack stations) hands out work; each robot's whole job, to the pick face, to a station and home, is planned against every other robot's reservations by safe-interval path planning; the floor executes and its collision checker inspects every robot every second.

steps.title: Two aisles blocked, a charger fails
steps.say: The generator is told a forklift blocks aisle C-14 ten seconds in, a spill closes B-27 thirty seconds later, and charger CH-05 fails at seventy. The orchestrator learns of each only as it happens: robots due into a closed aisle are re-planned around it (a robot inside finishes its pick and leaves), orders whose pick face is in it are held rather than failed, and the robot charging on CH-05 rejoins the charging queue.

steps.title: Pause a robot in traffic
steps.say: An operator stops the robot standing in the aisle cell the most other robots are due through. It becomes an obstacle: every robot due through its cell within 30 seconds is re-planned at once, the rest at the next dispatch epoch. The close-up shows the next 40 seconds of the robots re-planned at once, before and after.

body.reason: operator stop: robot reported a snagged tote

steps.title: Five urgent orders
steps.say: The WMS sends five urgent orders with a two-minute SLA, deep in block A and far from the pack stations, and a sixth with a location that does not exist, which is refused. The fleet engineer asks for a recompute: the current plan and a preemptive one, taking robots already near the urgent picks off ordinary orders, are projected four minutes ahead on a copy of the floor that knows no future orders. Preemption gets more urgent orders out on time but takes robots off their work, so it becomes a proposal.

steps.title: A second person approves
steps.say: The engineer cannot approve it; the shift manager does. The plan applies only because the floor has not moved since it was computed. The stopped robot is released, and the floor runs four more minutes: the urgent orders' delivery times sit beside the projection.

steps.title: The same shift under FIFO
steps.say: The same shift start, the same 7.5 minutes of orders and the same disruptions run in a sandbox three times, changing only the dispatcher: FIFO (the oldest order to the nearest free robot), greedy best pair, and CP-SAT. Then the audit trail: every load, advance, stop, order, plan, approval and simulation, hash-chained.
